blocks.title: Food hygiene
blocks.md: **Food hygiene** means keeping food safe to eat. Germs (**bacteria**, viruses, moulds) on hands, surfaces, flies, dirty water or raw meat can contaminate food and cause **food poisoning** with stomach pain, vomiting and diarrhoea.

blocks.title: Rules
blocks.md:
- **Wash hands** with soap and clean water before cooking and after using the toilet or touching raw meat or fish.
- Keep long hair tied and nails clean; cover cuts.
- Wash fruit and vegetables.
- Keep raw and cooked food **separate**; use different knives and boards.
- Cook food thoroughly and keep it covered; store leftovers safely and heat them well.
- Use clean (boiled or treated) water.

blocks.caption: A table of four hygiene actions to do and to avoid.
blocks.alt: Table of do and do-not food hygiene rules.

blocks.title: Kitchen safety
blocks.md: Turn pan handles inwards; keep children away from fire; do not leave cooking unattended; dry hands before touching electrical items; keep knives sharp and cut away from your body; clean up spills; store gas cylinders safely and check for leaks as taught by a qualified person.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Food left in warm conditions for hours can make people ill even if it smells normal.
- A cloth used for everything spreads germs.
- First aid advice must come from a trained person. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Raw chicken was cut on a board. Then the same board was used for salad. What is wrong and what should be done?
steps: Germs from raw chicken can pass to the salad (cross-contamination).
Use separate boards or wash the board well with hot soapy water before using it for ready-to-eat food.
blocks.answer: Cross-contamination: separate boards or wash well

blocks.title: Why cook?
blocks.md: Cooking makes food **safer** (kills many germs), **easier to chew and digest**, **tastier** and sometimes longer-lasting. But cooking can also **reduce some vitamins**, so use suitable methods and times.

blocks.title: Methods
blocks.md: **Boiling** in bubbling water (cassava, plantain, eggs). **Steaming** over water (moin-moin, vegetables). **Frying** in hot oil (puff-puff, fried plantain, fish). **Roasting/grilling** by dry heat (corn, plantain, fish). **Baking** in an oven (bread, cakes). **Stewing** slowly in a sauce (ndolé, stews).

blocks.caption: A table of four cooking methods with local examples.
blocks.alt: Table: boiling cassava and eggs, steaming moin-moin, frying puff-puff and fish, roasting corn and plantain.

blocks.title: Choosing a method
blocks.md: Boiling and steaming add no fat; steaming keeps more vitamins than boiling in a lot of water. Frying adds fat and energy; use fresh oil and do not reuse it many times. Grilling can be a lighter method if food is not burnt.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Burnt or blackened food should not be eaten often.
- Keep fat for frying at a safe temperature; hot oil can cause serious burns.
- Cassava (especially bitter types) must be well processed and cooked as traditionally done. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Which method is best to cook green vegetables to keep their vitamins?
steps: Long boiling in much water loses vitamins.
Steaming or cooking quickly with little water keeps more of them.
blocks.answer: Steam or cook quickly with little water

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Name the cooking method for each: (a) puff-puff, (b) boiled plantain, (c) roasted corn.
steps: (b) Boiling in water. (c) Roasting over heat.

Smoking fish: health concerns about smoke compounds exist; wording is simplified and should be reviewed.

blocks.title: Why preserve?
blocks.md: Food spoils because of **microorganisms** (bacteria, yeasts, moulds) and **enzymes**. Preservation **slows or stops spoilage** so food lasts longer, reduces waste, keeps food available out of season and helps trade.

blocks.title: Methods
blocks.md: **Drying** removes water (dried fish, crayfish, maize, beans). **Smoking** dries and adds protective substances (smoked fish and meat). **Salting** draws out water (salted fish). **Refrigeration** (cold) slows growth of germs; **freezing** nearly stops it. **Canning** heats food in sealed containers. **Sugar** and **pickling** (vinegar) are also used.

blocks.caption: A table of four preservation methods, what each removes or does, and an example.
blocks.alt: Table: drying removes water, smoking dries with smoke, cold removes warmth, canning removes germs and air.

blocks.title: How they work
blocks.md: Microorganisms need **water, warmth, food, time and (often) air**. Preservation takes away one or more of these: drying removes water; cold removes warmth; canning kills germs and seals out air; salt and sugar make water unavailable.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Preserved food can still spoil if stored badly (damp, hot).
- Do not eat swollen or leaking cans or food with mould.
- Dry grains and groundnuts well and store them dry to avoid harmful moulds. Nutrition and health statements are general, textbook-level and conservative: a dietitian or health worker must review them before release.

blocks.title: Example 1
blocks.statement: Why does dried fish last longer than fresh fish?
steps: Drying removes most of the water, so germs cannot grow.

blocks.title: Example 2
blocks.statement: Name a method to keep milk for several days in a home with a fridge and explain.
steps: Low temperature slows the growth of germs; it does not make milk last forever.
